title: HTML Mastery Challenge
subtitle: The Final Test: Think Like a Professional Developer
description: Review the HTML skills from Lessons 1–9, learn a few essential professional details, and answer 20 challenging application-based questions.

blocks.title: Welcome to Your Final HTML Challenge
blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 10! Today, you will test your mind. You have completed the main HTML learning journey, and now it is time to prove how well you can apply what you have learned. This is not simply a test of memorized definitions. You will examine code, identify problems, choose the best solutions, and think through situations that real developers encounter. There are exactly 20 questions: two questions reviewing each of Lessons 1–10. Read every option carefully because several answers may appear reasonable, but only one is the best answer for the situation described. Do not rush. A strong developer understands not only what works, but also why it works and when another approach would be better.

blocks.title: Important HTML Knowledge Every Developer Should Know
blocks.text:
HTML describes the structure and meaning of web content. Browsers parse HTML into a Document Object Model (DOM), a tree-like representation that JavaScript and browser tools can inspect. The HTML source you write and the live DOM shown in developer tools may differ because the browser can repair certain markup errors or scripts can change the page after loading. HTML also has void elements, which do not have closing tags. Common examples include ,
, , , and . Do not write an ordinary closing tag for these elements. Correct nesting matters: close elements in the proper order so the document structure is predictable. Comments written as help developers explain code, but they are not a place for passwords, secret keys, private information, or security rules. Anyone who can access a page's source may be able to read its comments. Likewise, hiding a form field with CSS does not make its value secret or trustworthy. HTML forms describe user input and submission, but HTML alone does not securely process or store that information. A server must validate submitted data independently. Browser validation improves usability; it is not a replacement for server-side validation. For links that open new tabs, use target="_blank" thoughtfully and add rel="noopener" where appropriate to prevent the new page from controlling the original page through window.opener. Never assume that a link, form field, or hidden input is safe just because it is written in HTML.

blocks.title: Paths, Special Characters, and Reliable Markup
blocks.text:
Paths determine where browsers find resources. A relative path such as images/logo.png is resolved from the current document's URL, while an absolute URL such as https://example.com/images/logo.png identifies a resource using its full address. A leading slash refers to the site root, which can behave differently when a site is hosted inside a subdirectory. Check paths carefully after deployment because a file that works on your local device may not be available at the same URL online.

Some characters have special meaning in HTML. For example, use &lt; to display a literal less-than sign and &amp; to display an ampersand when needed in text. Use quotes around attribute values, and escape user-provided text when inserting it into HTML through JavaScript. Treating untrusted input as HTML can create cross-site scripting (XSS) risks. HTML is not a security boundary: the application must handle untrusted data safely.

Finally, validate your document and test it in a browser. Check headings, links, keyboard access, image alternatives, form labels, mobile layout, missing resources, and browser-console errors. A page that looks correct on one screen is not automatically accessible, valid, secure, or ready for deployment.

blocks.title: Sample 2: A Form with Clear Labels and Button Types
blocks.code:
<form action="/contact" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <label for="message">Message</label>
  <textarea id="message" name="message" required></textarea>

  <button type="submit">Send message</button>
  <button type="button" onclick="alert('Draft saved locally only')">
    Preview action
  </button>
</form>
blocks.output: The first button submits the form. The second button performs a separate action and does not submit the form because its type is explicitly button. The server endpoint must still validate submitted data.

blocks.title: Sample 3: Displaying Text Without Treating It as HTML
blocks.output: The entered value is displayed as text. Using textContent avoids interpreting the value as HTML markup, which is safer than inserting untrusted input with innerHTML.

blocks.title: Your 20-Question Challenge Begins Now
blocks.text: You are about to answer 20 questions covering the full learning journey. Questions 1–2 review Lesson 1, questions 3–4 review Lesson 2, and so on, through questions 19–20 for Lesson 10. Each question has four close options. Choose the single best answer based on the code and situation provided. If you are uncertain, reason from the browser's behavior, document structure, accessibility, reliability, and security. Your goal is not merely to finish; it is to demonstrate sound judgment. Take a breath, read carefully, and begin.

blocks.question: A page contains headings and paragraphs, but the browser displays unexpected characters and does not interpret the document as intended. Which starting point is the most reliable for a modern HTML document?
options: Start with <body> and place the title inside the first paragraph.
Use <!doctype html>, then the html element containing head and body.
Put all metadata and visible content inside the head element.
Use <html5> and <page> elements to tell the browser the document type.
blocks.explanation: The doctype declares the modern HTML document mode, and the html element contains the head and body. The head holds document metadata, while the body contains the page's visible content.
blocks.hint: Think about the standard document skeleton and the separate jobs of head and body.

blocks.question:
A developer writes

Learn HTML

. The page seems to display, but the markup is improperly nested. What is the best correction?
options: Remove every closing tag because browsers can infer the structure.
Replace strong with a second p element and leave the order unchanged.

Close strong before closing p:

Learn HTML

.
Move the closing p tag into the document head.
blocks.explanation: Nested elements should be closed in the reverse order in which they were opened. Correct nesting creates a predictable document structure even if a browser attempts to recover from malformed markup.
blocks.hint: The most recently opened nested element should normally be closed first.

blocks.question: A learner needs the main heading of an article to be meaningful to browsers, assistive technology, and other developers. Which choice is best?
options:
Use
Article title
because appearance defines meaning.

Use

Article title

for the main page heading, then organize subordinate headings logically.

Use

Article title

because bold text always behaves as a heading.
Use an image of the words because images are automatically more accessible.
blocks.explanation: Heading elements express document hierarchy. CSS can change appearance, but styling a div or paragraph does not automatically give it heading semantics.
blocks.hint: Choose the element that communicates the purpose of the text, not just its appearance.

blocks.question: A website's navigation link works on the developer's computer but fails after deployment. The page is at /academy/lessons/intro.html and the link is href="images/logo.png". The image is actually at /academy/images/logo.png. Which fix matches the stated locations?
options: Use href="/images/logo.png" because a leading slash always means the current folder.
Use href="images/logo.png" because all relative paths start at the site root.
Use href="../images/logo.png" to move up one directory before entering images.
Use href="./../..//images/logo.png" because extra slashes repair paths.
blocks.explanation: The current page is in /academy/lessons/. The path ../images/logo.png moves to /academy/ and then enters images. A leading slash would point to /images/logo.png at the domain root, which is not the stated location.
blocks.hint: Resolve the relative path from the folder containing the current HTML document.

blocks.question: A product image conveys information that is not written anywhere else on the page. What should the developer do to make the image's purpose available to people who cannot see it?
options: Give the image a useful alt description of the information it conveys.
Use loading="lazy" because lazy loading automatically describes images.
Add a title attribute and omit alt because screen readers always prefer title.
Put the description only in a CSS background declaration.
blocks.explanation: Meaningful images need concise, useful alternative text. Lazy loading affects when an image is loaded, not its accessible description. CSS background images do not provide the same built-in alt-text mechanism.
blocks.hint: Separate image-loading performance from the text alternative for image content.

blocks.question: A video is essential to a lesson, and some learners need captions to understand its spoken content. Which approach is best?
options: Use autoplay with muted audio; muting automatically creates captions.
Place the video inside a table so the browser generates a transcript.
Provide a captions track, such as a correctly configured <track kind="captions">, with a suitable captions file.
Use alt on the video element because alt provides synchronized captions.
blocks.explanation: A captions track provides synchronized text for spoken audio and relevant sound information. Muting, tables, and image alt attributes do not create video captions.
blocks.hint: Look for the HTML feature designed to supply timed text for media.

blocks.question: A developer is showing three steps in a procedure where the order matters. Which markup best communicates that sequence?
options: A ul element, because every list represents an ordered process.
An ol element containing one li for each step.
Three br elements with the steps written after each break.
A table with no row or column headings, because tables define sequence.
blocks.explanation: An ordered list communicates a sequence where the order matters. Each list item belongs inside the ol element.
blocks.hint: Choose the list element that expresses sequence rather than an unordered collection.

blocks.question: A page presents prices for several products, with each product's price aligned under a column heading. Which structure is most appropriate for this genuinely tabular data?
options: Use a table with rows, header cells such as th, and data cells such as td.
Use a series of nested headings because headings automatically align data into columns.
Use a definition list because every price is a definition of a product.
Use a single pre element because fixed-width text is always the most accessible table.
blocks.explanation: A table is appropriate for data with meaningful row-and-column relationships. Header cells help communicate those relationships, while CSS can handle visual alignment.
blocks.hint: The content has a real row-and-column relationship, not just a visual layout.

blocks.question: A registration form contains an input with id="email" but no name attribute. The user submits the form using the default browser form submission. What is the key problem?
options: The browser refuses to display any input without a name.
The id attribute automatically becomes the submitted field name in every form.
The field may be omitted from the submitted form data because successful controls generally need a name.
The form is automatically encrypted because the field is an email input.
blocks.explanation: The id connects the control to labels and scripts, while name supplies the key used in normal form submission. An input type does not automatically encrypt its value.
blocks.hint: Distinguish the attribute used to identify an element in the document from the attribute used in submitted form data.

blocks.question: A form has a button labeled "Preview" that should run a preview action without submitting the form. Which choice is the most reliable?
options: Use <button type="submit">Preview</button> and assume its label prevents submission.
Use <button type="button">Preview</button> and attach the preview behavior separately.
Use <input type="email"> because email inputs never submit forms.
Remove the form element; a button cannot work inside a form.
blocks.explanation: A button inside a form defaults to submit behavior in common HTML form contexts when no type is specified. Explicitly setting type="button" prevents it from submitting the form by default.
blocks.hint: Choose the button type that does not perform form submission.

blocks.question: A developer marks the main content area with <div id="main">. They want to improve the document's semantic structure without changing the visual design. Which is generally the best improvement?
options: Replace every div on the page with an article, regardless of its purpose.
Use <main> for the page's dominant main content and retain div where no semantic element fits.
Use <footer> for the main content because it appears near the bottom on mobile screens.
Use <nav> around all page content so assistive technology can find it.
blocks.explanation: The main element identifies the dominant content of the page. Semantic elements should be selected according to meaning, not used indiscriminately to replace every generic container.
blocks.hint: Select the element whose defined purpose matches the dominant content area.

blocks.question: A form control has a visible text label, but clicking the label does not focus the control. The label's for value is "phoneNumber", while the input's id is "phone". What is the best fix?
options: Change the label's for value to "phone" so it matches the input id.
Change the input name to "phoneNumber"; name must always match the label.
Add aria-hidden="true" to the input to make the label work.
Wrap the whole page inside the label element.
blocks.explanation: A label's for attribute must match the id of the control it labels. The name attribute serves a different purpose and does not establish this explicit label association.
blocks.hint: Compare the label's for attribute with the input's id, character by character.

blocks.question: A developer wants a mobile page to use the device's viewport width rather than a wide desktop-style layout scaled down by the browser. Which head element is the standard choice?
options: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
<meta name="mobile" content="make everything responsive">
<meta charset="responsive">
<viewport width="device-width">
blocks.explanation: The viewport meta element tells mobile browsers how to set the layout viewport. Responsive CSS is still needed to adapt the design to different screen sizes.
blocks.hint: The standard uses a meta element with a particular name and content value.

blocks.question: A developer adds <script src="app.js" defer></script> in the document head. What is the best description of defer for a classic external script?
options: It executes the script before the HTML parser starts, regardless of network speed.
It prevents the script from ever executing unless the user clicks a button.
It lets HTML parsing continue while the script downloads, then executes the script after parsing and before DOMContentLoaded.
It converts the JavaScript file into HTML and places it inside the head.
blocks.explanation: A classic external script with defer downloads without blocking HTML parsing and executes after parsing is complete, preserving document order among deferred classic scripts. Module scripts have their own deferred-by-default behavior.
blocks.hint: Focus on the relationship between downloading, HTML parsing, and script execution.

blocks.question: A website owner wants search engines and social platforms to understand a page when it is shared. Which approach is the most appropriate?
options: Use a descriptive title and meta description, plus suitable Open Graph metadata when social previews are needed.
Put the entire page's text inside the meta description and omit the body.
Use only a favicon because it replaces page metadata in search results.
Add multiple identical title elements to increase the page's search ranking.
blocks.explanation: A meaningful title and description provide useful page metadata. Open Graph fields can help define social-sharing previews. Duplicate titles do not improve the page's quality.
blocks.hint: Choose the combination that serves both page identification and social-sharing previews.

blocks.question: A developer adds loading="lazy" to the main hero image, which is immediately visible at the top of the page. The image now appears later than expected. What is the best adjustment?
options: Keep lazy loading on every image because it always improves the first visible content.
Remove the image alt text so the browser downloads the file faster.
Convert the image into a heading because headings load before images.
Consider loading the important above-the-fold image eagerly and reserve lazy loading for suitable off-screen images.
blocks.explanation: Lazy loading can reduce unnecessary early downloads for off-screen images, but delaying a prominent image can harm perceived performance. Choose loading behavior according to the image's role and position.
blocks.hint: Consider whether the image is needed immediately when the page first appears.

blocks.question: A course website works locally, but the deployed version has a missing stylesheet, a broken image, and a link that points to a file on the developer's device. What is the best next step?
options: Assume the browser will upload the missing local files automatically.
Inspect the deployed URLs and network errors, correct the resource paths, ensure required files are deployed, and retest.
Replace all resource URLs with random absolute URLs until one works.
Remove the head element because it prevents the browser from finding stylesheets.
blocks.explanation: Deployment problems often come from missing files, incorrect paths, or references to resources that only exist locally. Inspect the actual deployed requests, fix the paths and deployment contents, and test again.
blocks.hint: Debug the resources the deployed browser is actually trying to request.

blocks.question: A developer finishes a capstone site. The pages look attractive, but some links fail, keyboard users cannot identify form controls, and a heading level was chosen only for its font size. What should happen before the project is considered ready?
options: Only increase the font sizes because appearance is the main measure of HTML quality.
Add more decorative div elements to hide the structural problems.
Test links and keyboard navigation, associate labels with controls, correct heading structure, validate the markup, and retest.
Deploy immediately because browsers automatically correct every accessibility and usability issue.
blocks.explanation: A professional review includes functionality, semantics, accessibility, validation, and real-browser testing. Visual polish alone does not establish that a site is usable or correct.
blocks.hint: Think of readiness as more than visual design: functionality, semantics, accessibility, and validation all matter.

blocks.question: A developer places a database password in an HTML comment so it is not visible on the page. Which statement is correct?
options: It is safe because browsers hide all HTML comments from visitors.
It is safe if the comment is placed inside the head element.
It is safe if the password is written using HTML character entities.
It is not safe: comments can be inspected in page source, so secrets must not be placed in client-side HTML.
blocks.explanation: HTML comments are part of the delivered source and are not a secure storage mechanism. Secrets such as database credentials must be kept on trusted server-side systems and protected appropriately.
blocks.hint: Ask whether a visitor can inspect the HTML source sent to their browser.

blocks.question: A search box displays user-provided text. A developer uses result.innerHTML = userInput, and a security reviewer warns that the input could contain HTML markup. Which change is the safest default when the intention is to display the input as plain text?
options: Use result.textContent = userInput so the browser treats the value as text rather than parsing it as HTML.
Use result.outerHTML = userInput because replacing the element automatically removes dangerous markup.
Place the input inside an HTML comment and then copy it into the page.
Use a hidden input field because hidden values cannot contain markup.
blocks.explanation: textContent inserts the value as text instead of parsing it as HTML, reducing the risk of cross-site scripting in this display scenario. Other contexts and server-side handling still require appropriate validation and output handling.
blocks.hint: Choose the DOM property intended to set text content without interpreting it as markup.
